entities.name: William de la Mare
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William de la Mare, an English Franciscan theologian who died in 1290, emerged as a pivotal figure in the late 13th-century scholastic debates, primarily known for his vehement critique of the burgeoning Thomist intellectual system. Operating within the vibrant intellectual centers of Oxford and Paris, de la Mare became a leading voice of the more conservative Franciscan tradition, deeply concerned that the philosophical innovations of Thomas Aquinas, particularly regarding the unity of substantial form and the nature of the soul, deviated dangerously from established Augustinian thought and posed a threat to the purity of Christian doctrine. His work crystallized the intellectual tensions between the Dominican and Franciscan orders, shaping the contours of scholastic discourse for decades.

De la Mare's most enduring and controversial achievement was the *Correctorium fratris Thomae* (Correction of Friar Thomas), a systematic catalog and refutation of 117 propositions found in Aquinas's writings, compiled around 1278. This meticulously argued text challenged core Thomist tenets, including the unicity of substantial form in man, the nature of angels, and the relationship between faith and reason, asserting their incompatibility with traditional Augustinian and Bonaventurian theology. The *Correctorium* was not merely an academic exercise; it became an official text within the Franciscan Order, mandated for study and used to guide Franciscan students away from what was perceived as Thomist error, thus institutionalizing a critical stance against the Dominican master.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: William de la Mare's *Correctorium fratris Thomae* significantly shaped late 13th-century scholasticism by institutionalizing a major critique of Thomist philosophy within the Franciscan Order, thereby influencing subsequent theological developments across continental Europe.
